expectations.text: The article reports 300 messages, 20 work requests, and 5 runs.
expectations.evidence: outputs/article.md:43 states the fixed load was 300 messages and 20 work requests with 5 runs; the same figures are also summarized in :7 and :48.

expectations.text: The article preserves all supplied performance and cache measurements.
expectations.evidence: outputs/article.md:5, :31, :37, :43, :48, and :50-52 preserve the 2.5-second batching window, average batch size 2.8, 2.5-to-3.9-second call time, 1.6 seconds per request, cache tokens 2323万-to-3177万, new-scheme p50 12.4 minutes, new-scheme p95 15.7 minutes, and control p95 29.5 minutes.

expectations.text: The article explains the naive approach and Router/Worker tradeoffs.
expectations.evidence: outputs/article.md:9-13 explains that the naive approach leaves tracking pressure with one person and reaches its limit at 3-5 sessions. outputs/article.md:15-33 explains batching and the tradeoff between a slower single call (2.5 to 3.9 seconds) and lower per-request amortization (1.6 seconds), including low-load waiting.

expectations.text: The article preserves low-load waiting and prompt-prefix stability as negative results, including the undecided low-load policy.
expectations.evidence: outputs/article.md:7, :33, :39, :65-66, and :70-73 explicitly state the extra 2.5-second low-load wait, the dependency on stable prompt prefixes, and that automatic shortening of the low-load window has not been decided.

expectations.text: The article limits conclusions to the supplied workload and identifies unknowns.
expectations.evidence: outputs/article.md:3, :41-54, and :74-78 limit the result to 300 messages, 20 work requests, and 5 runs; explicitly reject extrapolation to other workloads; and identify missing timing definitions, raw run values, variance, cache metrics, ablations, and module details.

expectations.text: The article does not promote unsupplied Router/Worker responsibilities or implementation details to confirmed facts.
expectations.evidence: outputs/article.md:17-29 labels only the window-batching relationship as confirmed and explicitly says Router/Worker responsibilities, communication, queue structure, failure handling, and scheduling rules were not provided. outputs/article.md:76 repeats this boundary.

claims.claim: The article's measured result is a p95 change from 29.5 minutes for the control group to 15.7 minutes for the new scheme under the stated workload.
claims.evidence: outputs/article.md:45-50 gives the control p95 as 29.5 minutes and the Router/Worker p95 as 15.7 minutes, and :54 limits the comparison to the fixed workload and 5 runs.

claims.claim: The observed cache-token increase can be converted directly into monetary savings or attributed entirely to batching.
claims.evidence: The article explicitly rejects this claim at outputs/article.md:37 and :52 because no token prices, total token consumption, cache hit rate, or causal split were supplied.

claims.claim: The article reports the Router and Worker internal responsibilities, communication method, queue structure, failure handling, and scheduling rules as known design facts.
claims.evidence: This claim is contradicted by outputs/article.md:29 and :76, which mark all of those implementation details as unavailable.

claims.claim: The article preserves the tradeoff that a single model call becomes slower while the supplied per-request amortization improves.
claims.evidence: outputs/article.md:31 and :56-68 state the 2.5-to-3.9-second single-call increase alongside the supplied 1.6-second per-request figure and explain the bounded tradeoff.

claims.claim: A deepseek-flash-style scan found no HIGH findings and retained one MEDIUM finding.
claims.evidence: The executor transcript reports this at transcript.md:22, but no scan report or other scan artifact is present in the output directory, so the result cannot be independently inspected.

suggestions.assertion: The article preserves all supplied performance and cache measurements.
suggestions.reason: This checks numerical preservation but not whether the article gives the requested cost accounting. Add an assertion requiring the article to distinguish latency, token measurements, and monetary cost, and to avoid inventing prices or savings.

No assertion directly checks that the Markdown deliverable is suitable for engineers outside the team or that it explains the requested experiment methodology, limitations, and open questions in a usable structure. Add a content-quality assertion covering audience framing and those sections.

eval_feedback.overall: The six assertions are substantively satisfied and are not merely filename or keyword checks. The main gap is that cost treatment, external-reader usability, and explicit open-question coverage are only indirectly tested.
